reason: The quote under 'Ways to use Lambda@Edge' says a Lambda function can make network calls to external resources to confirm user credentials or fetch additional content to customize a response; the claim matches.

Under 'Lambda features' the page lists as not supported: VPC access configuration, Lambda environment variables (except reserved ones) and functions with more than 512 MB ephemeral storage. All three parts are quoted.
The quote states Lambda@Edge is not supported with gRPC requests, same scope and wording.
Under 'Lambda function version' the page says you must use a numbered version, not $LATEST or aliases.
The Origin request entry says the function runs only when CloudFront forwards a request to the origin and does not run when the object is in the cache.
The Origin response entry says it runs after the origin response and before caching, even if the origin returns an error.
Under 'Lambda Region' the page says the Lambda function must be in US East (N. Virginia).
Under 'Lambda role permissions' the quote names both service principals that must be allowed to assume the role.
The page lists these three items as use cases for which Lambda@Edge is ideal; the claim restates them with the same scope.
The Viewer request entry says the function runs when CloudFront receives a viewer request, before it checks the cache.
The Viewer response entry says it runs before returning the file, regardless of whether the file is in the cache.
Under 'HTTP status codes' the page says viewer response functions cannot modify the HTTP status code of the response.

The quotes cover A/B testing with cookies and URL rewrites, HTTP responses at viewer or origin request, and header or token inspection, but the clause 'return different objects by device' appears only in the surrounding bullet, not in any quote.
Under the CachingDisabled heading the page says the policy disables caching and is useful for dynamic content and non-cacheable requests.
Under CachingOptimized the page says it minimizes cache key values, includes no query strings or cookies and only the normalized Accept-Encoding header.
Quote states GET and HEAD are cached, OPTIONS optionally, and other methods are not cached.
Quote: for gRPC you must select GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE, because gRPC requires POST.
Under Minimum TTL the warning says with minimum TTL above 0 CloudFront caches for at least that duration even with no-cache, no-store or private directives.
The quote says with mutual TLS you can make sure only clients presenting trusted TLS certificates gain access to your distributions.
Optional mode validates the certificate if presented but allows connections without one; exact match.
Passthrough mode does not validate against a trust store, forwards the certificate as HTTP headers, and needs no trust store; all stated in the quote.
Required mode is marked (default); it validates against a trust store and denies the connection if validation fails or no certificate is presented.
Quote says certificate validation happens at AWS edge locations, offloading authentication from the origin servers.

The quote supports no routing endpoint, no direct access and the need for a connection group and tenants, but the word 'template' (that a multi-tenant distribution is a template) is not in the quote, only implied by the context.
Quotes state each new website gets a tenant that inherits the source distribution values, then customizes settings, and that a tenant supports an individual domain or subdomain.
Quote: with OAC, communication to S3 is always through HTTPS, but only when you choose to always sign requests.
Quote names the cloudfront.amazonaws.com principal and a Condition limiting access to requests on behalf of the distribution with the S3 origin.
Quote: OAC doesn't support origin redirect by using Lambda@Edge.
Quote: CloudFront provides OAC for restricting access to a Lambda function URL origin.
Quote states PUT or POST with a Lambda function URL needs the SHA256 of the body in x-amz-content-sha256, and Lambda doesn't support unsigned payloads; under the OAC setup section for Lambda.
The quote supports 'must be publicly accessible' and 'CloudFront cannot access the origin', but 'passes the S3 errors on to viewers' is in the next sentence, not in the quote.
The quote, directly under the 'Do not override authorization header' setting, says to use it to sign origin requests only when the viewer request has no Authorization header.
Quotes state the two ways (OAC and OAI) and 'We recommend that you use OAC instead'.
Quote states OAC with S3 bucket origins requires Bucket owner enforced (the default for new buckets) and Bucket owner preferred if ACLs are required.
Quotes: a website-endpoint S3 origin is a custom origin, so you can't use OAC (or OAI); the context sentence gives the same chain.
Quote recommends Sign requests (always) and says CloudFront always signs all requests sent to the S3 origin.
The three quotes cover OAC support for all buckets in all Regions including opt-in Regions after December 2022, PUT and DELETE, and OAI not supporting these or needing workarounds.

The page says OAI does not support 'Amazon S3 buckets in all AWS Regions, including opt-in Regions', which means not all Regions; the claim says it does not support opt-in Regions at all, and the standalone quote for that item sits in the OAC supports list.
Quote states first allow both OAI and the OAC distribution, which makes sure CloudFront never loses access during the transition.
Quote defines a custom origin as an HTTP(S) web server with a publicly resolvable DNS name, hosted on AWS (for example EC2) or elsewhere.
Quote states private content is the exception; a signed URL can be used but the custom origin must remain publicly accessible.
Under 'HTTP port' for custom origins the valid values are 80, 443 and 1024 to 65535, default 80.
Under 'HTTPS port' for custom origins the valid values are 80, 443 and 1024 to 65535, default 443.
Quote lists the same examples of origin kinds, introduced with 'for example'.
Quote states an ALB, NLB or EC2 instance in a private subnet can be used as a VPC origin.
Under the heading 'Protocol (custom origins only)' the note says this applies only to custom origins.
Quote: HTTPS only means CloudFront uses only HTTPS to access the origin.
Quote states Match viewer uses HTTP or HTTPS depending on the viewer request protocol and caches the object only once.
Quote states HTTP only is the default for an S3 static website hosting endpoint because S3 doesn't support HTTPS for these endpoints.

The claim says query strings, headers and cookies are not included by default, but the next sentence gives an exception (with legacy cache settings CloudFront forwards headers by default) that is not in the quote.
Quote: you cannot use an origin request policy in a cache behavior without a cache policy.
The two quoted benefits state the origin is not publicly accessible and viewers reach content only through the specified distribution, not directly or via an unintended one.
Quote: CloudFront supports S3 origins using any storage class, including S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
Quotes state a website-endpoint S3 origin is a custom origin, and that creating it via the API requires CustomOriginConfig.
Under the heading for an S3 bucket configured as a website endpoint, the quote says you can use S3 redirects and custom error documents when the bucket is specified in the website endpoint format.
Quote says choose the Region with the lowest latency to your origin and that Origin Shield works with origins in an AWS Region and not in AWS.
Quote states requests for content not in Origin Shield's cache are consolidated, resulting in as few as one request to the origin.
Quotes state additional charges for Origin Shield, based on the number of requests going to Origin Shield as an incremental layer.
Quote states Origin Shield is an additional caching layer that minimizes origin load, improves availability and reduces operating costs.
Quote states Origin Shield isn't supported with gRPC, requests keep working but are proxied directly to the gRPC origin.
Quote lists dynamic content proxied to the origin, low cacheability and infrequently requested content as cases where it may not be a good fit.
Quote: requests made in the same Region as your origin will bypass Origin Shield.
Under 'Persistent connections' the page says CloudFront tries to maintain the connection for several seconds, saving TCP and TLS re-establishment.

The quotes support the IP ranges of origin-facing servers and allowing inbound traffic only from CloudFront, but 'maintained by CloudFront' and use in a VPC security group appear only in the surrounding text.
The quote sits in the Anycast Static IPs paragraph and states IPv4 addresses provided by AWS are charged $0.05 per IP address per hour.
Table row for Price Class 100 has Yes only for US/Mexico/Canada and Europe/Israel/Türkiye and x elsewhere, per the header.
Row has x only for South America and Australia/New Zealand, Yes for all other header columns; the claim matches.
Row for Price Class All has Yes in every column of the header.
Under 'Price class' the page says choose the class matching the maximum price you want to pay and that by default CloudFront serves from edge locations in all Regions.

Quote under Pricing states charges for data transfers out and HTTP or HTTPS requests, varying by usage type, geographical region and feature selection.

Quote states field-level encryption is charged based on the number of requests needing the additional encryption.
Quote under flat-rate benefits: blocked DDoS attacks and requests blocked by AWS WAF never count against your usage allowance.
FAQ quotes give Business plan $200/month with bot protection, advanced DDoS protection and private origin endpoints, and that plan prices do not vary by Region.
Table row Data Transfer shows 100GB, 50TB, 50TB and 50TB (configurable up to 600TB for a new flat-rate price) for Free, Pro, Business and Premium.
FAQ quotes: Free plan is $0/month, and each flat-rate plan includes global content delivery for one price (no regional variation).
FAQ quotes: Free Tier applies only to pay-as-you-go usage, and the Free flat-rate plan is one $0/month price.
